rejected.title: Static and current electricity
card: Static electricity
a build-up of electric charge on an object. The charge stays in one place, such as on a balloon after it is rubbed on hair.
Current electricity
a flow of charge through a conductor, such as a copper wire. A conductor is a material that lets charge move through it easily.
A voltage is what pushes charge around a circuit. A battery provides the voltage, and the charge flows only if the circuit is a complete loop.
Rubbing can make charge build up on an object. Sometimes the charge jumps away at once, as in a small spark.
rejected.remember: Static is charge that builds up. Current is charge that flows, pushed by a voltage.

a.q: Which of these is an example of current electricity?
opts: Charge flowing along the wires of a switched-on torch
Charge building up on a balloon rubbed on hair
Charge sitting on a plastic comb after combing
Charge collecting on a jumper rubbed on a rug
a.why: In a switched-on torch, charge flows through the wires, which are conductors, in a complete loop. That is current electricity. The balloon, comb and jumper all show static electricity, where charge builds up and stays on the object.
a.clue: Which example needs a conductor and a complete loop?

b.q: Leon connects a battery, a globe and wires in a complete loop, and the globe lights. What does the battery provide?
opts: A voltage that pushes charge around the loop
Static charge that builds up on the globe
Copper wire that lets the charge flow
Charge that is made by rubbing inside it
b.why: The battery provides the voltage, which pushes charge around the complete loop. The copper wire is the conductor that lets charge move, but the wires do that job, not the battery, and a conductor does not push the charge.
b.clue: Think about what makes charge move, not what lets it move.

a.q: Which of these describes current electricity?
opts: Charge flowing through a wire in a complete circuit
Charge building up on a balloon rubbed on hair
Charge staying still on a plastic ruler
Charge that cannot move through a conductor
a.why: Current electricity is a flow of charge through a conductor. Charge building up on a balloon is static electricity, because the charge stays in one place.
a.clue: Look for the option where charge is moving.

b.q: Leon connects a battery, a globe and wires in a complete loop and the globe lights. What is pushing the charge around the loop?
opts: The voltage from the battery
The static charge on the globe
The charge built up on the wires
The rubbing of the wires together
b.why: A voltage pushes charge around a complete circuit, and the battery provides it. Static charge is a build-up that stays in place, so it does not push the current.
b.clue: Which part of the circuit provides the push?

a.best: Charge flowing through a wire in a complete circuit

card: Static electricity
a build-up of electric charge on an object, such as a balloon after it is rubbed on hair. The charge stays on the object instead of flowing along a path.
Current electricity
a flow of charge through a conductor, such as a copper wire. A conductor is a material that lets charge move through it easily.
A voltage is what pushes charge around a circuit. A battery provides the voltage, and the charge flows only if the circuit is a complete loop.
Rubbing can make charge build up on an object. Built-up charge can suddenly jump away all at once, as a small spark.
version.remember: Static is charge that builds up. Current is charge that flows, pushed by a voltage.

a.q: Which of these shows current electricity?
opts: Charge moving through the wires of a lit torch
Charge building up on a child going down a slide
Charge sitting on a plastic comb after combing
Charge collecting on a jumper rubbed on a rug
a.why: In a lit torch, charge flows through the wires, which are conductors, in a complete loop. That is current electricity. The child, the comb and the jumper all show static electricity, where charge builds up and stays on the object.
a.clue: Which example needs a conductor and a complete loop?

b.q: Ana joins a battery, a globe and wires into a complete loop, and the globe lights up. What is the battery's job in this circuit?
opts: Giving a voltage that pushes charge around the loop
Storing static charge that builds up on the globe
Acting as a conductor that lets the charge flow
Making charge by rubbing parts together inside it
b.why: The battery provides the voltage, which pushes charge around the complete loop. Letting charge flow is the job of conductors such as the copper wires, and a conductor does not push the charge.
b.clue: Think about what makes charge move, not what lets it move.

b.best: Giving a voltage that pushes charge around the loop
